{{About|meaning in the number theory||Covering (disambiguation){{!}}Covering}}

In [[mathematics]], a '''covering set''' for a [[integer sequence|sequence of integers]] refers to a [[set (mathematics)|set]] of [[prime number]]s such that ''every'' term in the [[sequence]] is [[divisible]] by ''at least one'' member of the set.<ref>Guy, Richard; ''Unsolved Problems in Number Theory''; pp. 119–121. {{ISBN|0387208607}}</ref>  The term "covering set" is used only in conjunction with sequences possessing [[exponential growth]].

==Sierpinski and Riesel numbers==
The use of the term "covering set" is related to [[Sierpinski number|Sierpinski]] and [[Riesel number]]s. These are [[Even and odd numbers|odd]] [[natural number]]s {{mvar|k}} for which the formula {{math|''k'' 2<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;+&thinsp;1}} (Sierpinski number) or {{math|''k'' 2<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;−&thinsp;1}} (Riesel number) produces no prime numbers.<ref>Wells, David; ''Prime Numbers: The Most Mysterious Figures in Math''; pp. 212, 219. {{ISBN|1118045718}}</ref> Since 1960 it has been known that there exists an [[Infinity|infinite]] number of both Sierpinski and Riesel numbers (as solutions to families of [[congruence relation|congruences]] based upon the set {{nowrap|{3, 5, 17, 257, 641, 65537, 6700417}}}{{efn|These are of course the only known [[Fermat prime]]s and the two prime factors of F<sub>5</sub>.<ref>Sierpiński, Wacław (1960); ‘Sur un problème concernant les nombres’; ''[[Elemente der Mathematik]]'', 15(1960); pp. 73–96</ref>}} but, because there are an infinitude of numbers of the form {{math|''k'' 2<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;+&thinsp;1}} or {{math|''k'' 2<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;−&thinsp;1}} for any {{mvar|k}}, one can only [[mathematical proof|prove]] {{mvar|k}} to be a Sierpinski or Riesel number through showing that ''every'' term in the sequence {{math|''k'' 2<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;+&thinsp;1}} or {{math|''k'' 2<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;−&thinsp;1}} is divisible by one of the prime numbers of a covering set.

These covering sets form from prime numbers that in [[base 2]] have short periods. To achieve a complete covering set, [[Wacław Sierpiński]] showed that a sequence can repeat no more frequently than every 24 numbers. A repeat every 24 numbers give the covering set {{nowrap|{3, 5, 7, 13, 17, 241}}}, while a repeat every 36 terms can give several covering sets: {{nowrap|{3, 5, 7, 13, 19, 37, 73}}}; {{nowrap|{3, 5, 7, 13, 19, 37, 109}}}; {{nowrap|{3, 5, 7, 13, 19, 73, 109}}} and {{nowrap|{3, 5, 7, 13, 37, 73, 109}}}.<ref>[http://irvinemclean.com/maths/siercvr.htm Covering Sets for Sierpiński Numbers]</ref>

Riesel numbers have the same covering sets as Sierpinski numbers.

==Other covering sets==
Covering sets (thus Sierpinski numbers and Riesel numbers) also exists for [[radix|bases]] other than 2.<ref>[http://www.noprimeleftbehind.net/crus/Sierp-conjectures.htm Sierpinski conjectures and proofs]</ref><ref>[http://www.noprimeleftbehind.net/crus/Riesel-conjectures.htm Riesel conjectures and proofs]</ref><ref>[https://www.utm.edu/staff/caldwell/preprints/2to100.pdf Generalized Sierpinski number base b]</ref>

Covering sets are also used to prove the existence of composite [[Generalizations of Fibonacci numbers#Fibonacci integer sequences|generalized Fibonacci sequences]] with first two terms [[coprime]] ([[primefree sequence]]), such as the sequence starting with 20615674205555510 and 3794765361567513.

The concept of a covering set can easily be generalised to other sequences which turn out to be much simpler.

In the following examples + is used as it is in [[regular expression]]s to mean 1 or more. For example, 91<sup>+</sup>3 means the set {{nowrap|{913, 9113, 91113, 911113, …}}}.

An example are the following eight sequences:
* (29·10<sup>''n''</sup> −&thinsp;191) / 9 or 32<sup>+</sup>01
* (37·10<sup>''n''</sup> +&nbsp;359) / 9 or 41<sup>+</sup>51
* (46·10<sup>''n''</sup> +&nbsp;629) / 9 or 51<sup>+</sup>81
* (59·10<sup>''n''</sup> −&nbsp;293) / 9 or 65<sup>+</sup>23
* (82·10<sup>''n''</sup> +&thinsp;17) / 9 or 91<sup>+</sup>3
* (85·10<sup>''n''</sup> +&nbsp;41) / 9 or 94<sup>+</sup>9
* (86·10<sup>''n''</sup> +&nbsp;31) / 9 or 95<sup>+</sup>9
* (89·10<sup>''n''</sup> +&nbsp;593) / 9 or 98<sup>+</sup>23

In each case, every term is divisible by one of the primes from the set {{nowrap|{3, 7, 11, 13}}}.<ref>[http://www.worldofnumbers.com/deplat.htm Plateau and Depression Primes]</ref> These primes can be said to form a covering set exactly analogous to Sierpinski and Riesel numbers.<ref name="difficulty">[https://stdkmd.net/nrr/prime/primedifficulty.txt List of near-repdigit-related (probable) prime numbers, sorted by difficulty]</ref> The covering set {{nowrap|{3, 7, 11, 37}}} is found for several similar sequences,<ref name="difficulty"/> including:
* (38·10<sup>''n''</sup> −&thinsp;137) / 9 or 42<sup>+</sup>07
* (4·10<sup>''n''</sup> −&nbsp;337) / 9 or 4<sup>+</sup>07
* (73·10<sup>''n''</sup> +&nbsp;359) / 9 or 81<sup>+</sup>51

* 9175·10<sup>''n''</sup> +&thinsp;1 or 91750<sup>+</sup>1
* 10176·10<sup>''n''</sup> −&thinsp;1 or 101759<sup>+</sup>
* (334·10<sup>''n''</sup> −&thinsp;1)/9 or 371<sup>+</sup>
* (12211·10<sup>''n''</sup> −&thinsp;1)/3 or 40703<sup>+</sup>
* (8026·10<sup>''n''</sup> −&nbsp;7)/9 or 8917<sup>+</sup>

Also for bases other than 10:

* 521·12<sup>''n''</sup> +&thinsp;1 or 3750<sup>+</sup>1 in [[duodecimal]]
* (1288·12<sup>''n''</sup> −&thinsp;1)/11 or 991<sup>+</sup> in duodecimal
* (4517·12<sup>''n''</sup> −&nbsp;7)/11 or 2X27<sup>+</sup> in duodecimal
* 376·12<sup>''n''</sup> −&thinsp;1 or 273E<sup>+</sup> in duodecimal

The covering set of them is {{nowrap|{5, 13, 29}}}

An even simpler case can be found in the sequence:

* (76·10<sup>''n''</sup> −&nbsp;67) / 99 ('''''n'' must be odd''') or (76)<sup>+</sup>7 (Sequence: 7, 767, 76767, 7676767, 767676767 etc.)

Here, it can be shown that if:
* w is of form {{math|3''k''}} ({{math|1= ''n'' = 6''k'' + 1}}): (76)<sup>+</sup>7 is divisible by 7
* w is of form {{math|3''k'' + 1}} ({{math|1= ''n'' = 6''k'' + 3}}): (76)<sup>+</sup>7 is divisible by 13
* w is of form {{math|3''k'' + 2}} ({{math|1= ''n'' = 6''k'' + 5}}): (76)<sup>+</sup>7 is divisible by 3

Thus we have a covering set with only three primes {{nowrap|{3, 7, 13}}}.<ref>[http://www.worldofnumbers.com/undulat.htm Smoothly Undulating Palindromic Primes]</ref> This is only possible because the sequence gives integer terms ''only for odd n''.

A covering set also occurs in the sequence:

* (343·10<sup>''n''</sup> −&thinsp;1) / 9 or 381<sup>+</sup>.

Here, it can be shown that:
* If {{math|1= ''n'' = 3''k'' + 1}}, then {{math|(343·10<sup>''n''</sup> −&thinsp;1) / 9}} is divisible by 3.
* If {{math|1= ''n'' = 3''k'' + 2}}, then {{math|(343·10<sup>''n''</sup> −&thinsp;1) / 9}} is divisible by 37.
* If {{math|1= ''n'' = 3''k''}}, then {{math|(343·10<sup>''n''</sup> −&thinsp;1) / 9}} algebraically factors as {{math|((7·10<sup>''k''</sup> −&thinsp;1) / 3)·((49·10<sup>2''k''</sup> + 7·10<sup>''k''</sup> +&thinsp;1) / 3)}}.
Since {{math|(7·10<sup>''k''</sup> −&thinsp;1) / 3}} can be written as 23<sup>+</sup>, for the sequence 381<sup>+</sup>, we have a covering set of {3, 37, 23<sup>+</sup>} – a covering set with ''infinitely many'' terms.<ref name="difficulty"/>

The status for (343×10<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;−&thinsp;1)/9 is like that for 3511808×63<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;+&thinsp;1:

* If {{math|1= ''n'' = 3''k'' + 1}}, then {{math|3511808·63<sup>''n''</sup> +&thinsp;1}} is divisible by 37.
* If {{math|1= ''n'' = 3''k'' + 2}}, then {{math|3511808·63<sup>''n''</sup> +&thinsp;1}} is divisible by 109.
* If {{math|1= ''n'' = 3''k''}}, then {{math|3511808·63<sup>''n''</sup> +&thinsp;1}} algebraically factors as {{math|(152·63<sup>''k''</sup> +&thinsp;1)·(23104·63<sup>2''k''</sup> − 152·63<sup>''k''</sup> +&thinsp;1)}}

Thus we have a covering of {37, 109, 152×63 +&thinsp;1, 152×63<sup>2</sup> +&thinsp;1, 152×63<sup>3</sup> +&thinsp;1, ...} or {37, 109, 2Q0<sup>+</sup>1 in base 63} – a covering set with ''infinitely many'' terms.

A more simple example is 4×9<sup>''n''</sup> −&thinsp;1, it is equal to (2×3<sup>''n''</sup> −&thinsp;1) × (2×3<sup>''n''</sup> +&thinsp;1), thus its covering sets are {{nowrap|{5, 17, 53, 161, 485, ...}}} and {{nowrap|{7, 19, 55, 163, 487, ...}}}, more generally, if ''k'' and ''b'' are both ''r''-th powers for an odd ''r''&nbsp;>&thinsp;1, then ''k''×''b''<sup>''n''</sup> +&thinsp;1 cannot be prime, and if ''k'' and ''b'' are both ''r''-th powers for an ''r''&nbsp;>&thinsp;1 then ''k''×''b''<sup>''n''</sup> −&thinsp;1 cannot be prime.

Another example is 1369×30<sup>''n''</sup> −&thinsp;1, its covering is {7, 13, 19, 37×30<sup>''k''</sup> −&thinsp;1 (''k''&nbsp;=&thinsp;1, 2, 3, ...)}
